title: Short Stuff: Laughing Buddha
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Laughing Buddha, the jolly, pot-bellied figure often seen in Chinese restaurants and bars. The hosts explain that he is not the historical Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama, the teaching Buddha of this era) but Budai, a real tenth-century Chinese monk who wandered villages with a sack of treats for children and the poor. Budai was later regarded as a self-proclaimed incarnation of the future Buddha, Maitreya. The hosts cover bodhisattvas and avatars, the image spreading to the West through global trade and porcelain in the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries, and his association with restaurants, bartenders and the belly-rubbing tradition.

segments.title: Introduction to Buddhism and the Laughing Buddha
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a short look at Buddhism's laughing figure rather than the religion as a whole, noting prior episodes on Nirvana and karma and describing the statue seen in shops and restaurants.

segments.title: Siddhartha Gautama and the teaching Buddha
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the laughing figure is not the historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama (Shakyamuni), who achieved enlightenment under a Bodhi tree after meditating for 49 days. They note the term Buddha means awakened one and discuss the religion's roughly 400 million followers.

segments.title: Bodhisattvas, avatars and reincarnated Buddhas
segments.summary: The hosts describe bodhisattvas as devoted practitioners or enlightened beings who delay nirvana to help others, and explain the tradition of Buddhas being reborn in cycles, with Gautama the most recent of a line of 28 and later rebirths called avatars.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A brief break before the reveal of the Laughing Buddha's identity.

segments.title: Budai, the tenth-century monk
segments.summary: The hosts identify the Laughing Buddha as Budai, a real tenth-century Chinese monk who was pot-bellied and generous, traveling village to village with a sack of sweets and rice for children and the poor. His name is linked to the word for cloth sack, and he became a beloved figure associated with abundance and contentment.

segments.title: Future Buddha prophecy, spread to the West and belly rubbing
segments.summary: Budai reportedly wrote a poem on his deathbed claiming to be an incarnation of the next teaching Buddha, which cemented his place among deities. The image grew popular in art from about the fifteenth century and spread West through trade and porcelain, becoming a souvenir. The hosts discuss the tradition of rubbing his belly for luck and his patronage of restaurateurs and bartenders.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode and invite listeners to visit the website or email the show.
